issue.issue_text: Whether a procedural irregularity or illegality in conducting a search and seizure makes the evidence collected inadmissible.

law.law_text: In India, the law of evidence is modeled on English law, where the primary test for the admissibility of evidence is its relevancy.
Unlike the American legal system, Indian courts have consistently refused to exclude relevant evidence merely because it was obtained through an illegal search or seizure.

The Constitution Bench in 'Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection' held that unless there is an express prohibition in the Constitution or other law, evidence obtained from an illegal search is not to be excluded.
An illegality committed during an investigation does not, by itself, render the evidence obtained during that investigation inadmissible.

application.application_text: The Court reasoned that a procedural irregularity or illegality in a search and seizure does not automatically make the collected evidence inadmissible.
Instead of an automatic rule of exclusion, the trial court must consider all the circumstances of the case.
The key question for the court is to determine whether the procedural flaw caused any "serious prejudice" to the accused.

Evidence might be considered inadmissible only in extreme cases, such as when the search was in "complete defiance of the law" and created a possibility that the evidence was tampered with or interpolated.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a procedural irregularity or illegality in conducting a search and seizure does not, by itself, make the evidence inadmissible. The evidence is only to be excluded if the court finds, after considering all circumstances, that the irregularity caused serious prejudice to the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether a lapse or delayed compliance with the procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act would entitle an accused to be released on bail or vitiate the trial.

law.name: Section 52A, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
law.description: Lays down the procedure for the disposal and sampling of seized contraband substances.

law.name: Section 54, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
law.description: Creates a statutory presumption that an accused has committed an offence if they are found in possession of a narcotic drug and fail to account for it satisfactorily.

law.name: Section 37, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
law.description: Imposes strict, mandatory twin conditions for granting bail in serious NDPS offences, requiring the court to be satisfied that the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

application.point: The Court classified a lapse or delayed compliance with Section 52A as a mere "procedural irregularity," not a fatal "illegality." It reasoned that an irregularity, unlike an illegality, does not automatically nullify or vitiate the entire prosecution case.
The Court held that such a procedural lapse, by itself, is not a sufficient ground to grant bail or acquit an accused. It is only one factor to be considered among others.
The decision emphasized that courts must also consider all other primary evidence collected during the investigation. The case does not stand or fall solely on the compliance with Section 52A.

The Court pointed to the statutory presumption of guilt under Section 54 of the Act. It argued that it would be an "anomalous situation" to grant bail for a procedural issue (under Section 52A) when a strong presumption of guilt exists against an accused who possessed contraband and has not rebutted that presumption.
The Court also criticized the High Court for granting bail without satisfying the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, which it deemed a fundamental error.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a lapse or delay in complying with the procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act is a procedural irregularity that, by itself, neither vitiates the trial nor automatically entitles an accused to be released on bail. The court must consider this lapse in conjunction with other evidence and the statutory presumptions under the Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether granting bail under the NDPS Act is permissible without the court recording its satisfaction on the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b) of the Act.

facts: The High Court granted bail to an accused in a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act.
The sole reason for granting bail was the belated compliance with the procedure under Section 52A of the Act.
The High Court did not consider or record its findings on whether the twin conditions for bail under Section 37(1)(b) of the NDPS Act were met.
law: Section 37 of the NDPS Act contains mandatory provisions for granting bail in serious drug offenses.

For bail to be granted, a court must satisfy two cumulative conditions (the "twin conditions"): (i) there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty of the offense, and (ii) the accused is not likely to commit any offense while on bail.
The recording of the court's satisfaction on these twin conditions is a "sine qua non" (an essential prerequisite) for granting bail.
Under the NDPS Act, the general rule is the negation of bail, and its grant is an exception.
application: The Supreme Court found that it was obligatory for the High Court to assess and record its satisfaction regarding the twin conditions, especially since the prosecution (NCB) had opposed the bail application.
The High Court's failure to record this mandatory satisfaction rendered its order granting bail "fallacious and untenable."
The Court clarified that a procedural lapse, such as a delay in complying with Section 52A, is an "irregularity" that does not by itself vitiate the trial or automatically entitle an accused to bail.
Relying on a procedural irregularity to bypass the strict and mandatory bail conditions of Section 37 was deemed erroneous.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's approach, holding that granting bail under the NDPS Act is not permissible without the court explicitly recording its satisfaction on the mandatory twin conditions laid out in Section 37(1)(b). Since the High Court failed to do so, its order was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a procedural irregularity or illegality in conducting a search and seizure makes the evidence collected inadmissible.
appellant_arguments: A procedural irregularity or illegality in the search and seizure process does not, by itself, render the evidence collected inadmissible or vitiate the trial. The evidence obtained is still relevant and can be considered by the court.
respondent_arguments: Any illegality or failure to follow the prescribed procedure during a search and seizure taints the evidence collected, making it inadmissible in court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a lapse or delayed compliance with the procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act would entitle an accused to be released on bail or vitiate the trial.
appellant_arguments: The procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act, concerning the drawing of samples before a Magistrate, is primarily for creating primary evidence for trial. A delay or lapse in this procedure is a curable defect and does not automatically vitiate the entire proceedings or create a right for the accused to be granted bail.
respondent_arguments: Compliance with the procedure under Section 52A is mandatory. A failure to comply or a significant delay in compliance vitiates the seizure and the subsequent proceedings, which is a valid ground for granting bail to the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether granting bail under the NDPS Act is permissible without the court recording its satisfaction on the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b) of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The twin conditions for bail under Section 37(1)(b) of the NDPS Act are mandatory and must be satisfied before granting bail. A court cannot grant bail based on procedural lapses (like non-compliance with Section 52A) without first recording its satisfaction that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and will not commit an offense if released.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in granting bail. The non-compliance with the mandatory procedure of Section 52A is a significant factor that can form the basis for the court's satisfaction of the twin conditions under Section 37, particularly that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty.

cases.principle: For the principle of considering the scope of Section 37 in light of the scheme of the NDPS Act.

cases.case_name: Khet Singh vs. Union of India
cases.principle: For the principle that delayed compliance or non-compliance with the provision for disposal of seized substances is not an illegality that would entitle the accused to bail or acquittal, when sufficient material establishes that the search and seizure of the contraband was made in due compliance with the mandatory provisions of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Standing Orders are intended to guide officers to ensure a fair procedure is adopted during an investigation and are not to be treated as inexorable rules. Non-compliance may be permissible where circumstances make it impossible for the seizing officer to follow the procedure at the spot, such as in the case of a chance recovery.
obiter: Every law is designed to further the ends of justice and not to frustrate it on mere technicalities.

If the language of a Statute in its ordinary meaning and grammatical construction leads to a manifest contradiction of the apparent purpose of the enactment, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words, or even the structure of the sentence.
Where the main object and intention of a statute are clear, it must not be reduced to a nullity by the draftsman’s unskillfulness or ignorance of the law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order granting bail is fallacious and untenable because it was based on a procedural lapse—delayed compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act—without recording the mandatory satisfaction of the twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b) of the Act. A deviation or delay in the Section 52A procedure is merely a curable irregularity, not a fatal illegality that vitiates the prosecution's case or automatically entitles an accused to bail. Granting relief on such a technicality, while ignoring the stringent requirements of Section 37 and the statutory presumption of guilt under Section 54, would create an anomalous situation contrary to the legislative intent of the NDPS Act.
legal_tests_applied: The mandatory and cumulative twin conditions for bail under Section 37(1)(b) of the NDPS Act, requiring the court to record its satisfaction that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

The test for admissibility of evidence, which lies in its relevancy, meaning evidence obtained as a result of an illegal search and seizure is not liable to be shut out unless there is an express or implied prohibition in law.

The principle of statutory interpretation that a provision must be construed to avoid absurdity and mischief, and that the NDPS Act must be interpreted literally, not liberally, to uphold its object and purpose.
The statutory presumption of guilt under Section 54 of the NDPS Act, where the court presumes the accused has committed an offence unless the contrary is proved.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court erred in granting bail without recording its satisfaction on the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b), rendering its order fallacious and untenable.

The High Court incorrectly treated the delayed compliance with Section 52A as a ground for bail, whereas such a delay is merely an 'irregularity' and not an 'illegality which would nullify or vitiate the entire case of the prosecution'.

Granting bail on the basis of a procedural lapse under Section 52A creates an 'anomalous situation' where an accused, despite being found in possession of contraband and failing to rebut the statutory presumption of guilt under Section 54, is released, which 'could not be the intention of the legislature'.
why_respondent_won: It is settled law that an illegality committed during investigation, such as an illegal search and seizure, does not render the evidence obtained inadmissible; the test for admissibility is relevancy.

The twin conditions for bail under Section 37(1)(b) of the NDPS Act are mandatory and cumulative, and a court cannot grant bail for offences under the Act without first recording its satisfaction on both conditions.

A procedural lapse, such as a delay in following the Section 52A procedure, is a curable defect and cannot be treated as a persuasive ground for granting relief under the stringent bail provisions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act.
policy_considerations: The provisions of the NDPS Act must be interpreted literally and not liberally, keeping in mind its scheme, object, and purpose, to avoid frustrating the Preamble of the Act and to address its impact on society as a whole.
Every law is designed to further the ends of justice and not to frustrate it on 'mere technicalities'.
Statutory provisions must be construed, if possible, to avoid absurdity and mischief, and to produce a rational construction and just result.
The organized traffic in contraband has a 'deleterious effect on the national economy affecting the vitals of the economic life of the community'.
